query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled amount (e.g., ~5 at%) of aluminum into a refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., Mo-Nb-Ta-W based) and homogenizing by arc melting can improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the in-situ formation of a stable Al2O3 surface layer that reduces oxygen ingress and oxidation at ~1200°C in a 1 atm O2 environment.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., MoNbTaW) with negligible Al content, in the as-cast condition and without specialized oxidation-resistant modifications.
generation.intervention: Arc melting of the refractory alloy with ~5 atomic percent Al, followed by homogenization heat treatment at elevated temperature to ensure a uniform distribution of the added Al.
generation.conditions: Thermal cycling at approximately 1200°C in 1 atm O2 for up to 100 hours, representing extreme operating conditions relevant for structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, dense Al2O3 scale that forms on the alloy surface upon high-temperature exposure to oxygen.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature oxidation, aluminum selectively oxidizes at the surface, generating an impermeable Al2O3 layer that suppresses further oxygen penetration and minimizes substrate degradation, thereby slowing oxidation kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Mass gain and oxide scale thickness in the Al-doped alloy will be significantly lower (potentially reduced by over half) relative to the undoped baseline, indicating enhanced resistance to oxygen-induced degradation under extreme temperatures.
generation.baseline: An equivalent refractory high-entropy alloy with negligible Al content experiences more severe oxidation damage and scale spalling under the same conditions, evidenced by higher mass gain.
generation.boundary: Their performance may degrade if Al content exceeds ~10 at% or if the homogenization process is inadequate, risking brittle phase formation or inhomogeneous scales.
generation.uncertainty: While small Al additions are expected to form protective scales, the exact optimal doping level and potential mechanical trade-offs remain to be fully quantified by experiment.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from a baseline refractory HEA, one set without Al and the other with 5 at% Al added by arc melting. Subject both sets to identical homogenization and thermal cycling conditions at 1200°C in 1 atm O2 for 100 hours, periodically measuring mass change and characterizing surface oxides.
measurements: Mass gain (thermogravimetric analysis or differential weighing after exposure)
Characterization of oxide layer integrity and thickness (SEM cross-section, EDS elemental mapping)
XRD analysis of surface scale compositions
Hardness measurements before and after oxidation testing to detect any brittleness issues
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not exhibit a significantly lower mass gain and lacks a stable Al2O3-dominated surface scale relative to the baseline, or it shows unexpected oxide phases, the hypothesis is disproven.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most investigated HEA systems is AlCoCrCuFeNi and the copper-free derivate AlCoCrFeNi [,]. Distinct improvement of mechanical properties can be achieved by alloying with titanium. Due to its large atomic radius, the addition of titanium causes solid–solution strengthening and hence increased strength and hardness. Additionally, the formation of brittle phases was observed for a high content of titanium [,,]. The wear resistance of the alloy system AlCoCrFeNiTi has been investigated under various conditions revealing an increased wear resistance, also in comparison with the steels EN 1.3505 and EN 1.3343 [,]. Although improved high-temperature properties of AlCoCrFeNiTi are expected, the wear behaviour has not yet been investigated at increased temperature.
